title: Wales has a school standards crisis. Will plans to fix it actually work?
summary: Wales scores poorly on international test results but it is not clear a new curriculum will help.
full_text:
As you dip into the valley on the way into Merthyr Tydfil, a new earthy-toned building dominates the view.

It's the new site of Saint Carlo Acutis Catholic School. With its rooftop science garden, solar panels and floor-to-ceiling windows, it's an impressive sight.

Excited staff and 940 pupils moved into the £50m complex at the start of September. But they did so just as the Welsh education system was being painted in a less positive light, with Wales once again ranking the worst of UK nations in global tests.

"It casts doubt over a system we're proud of and children that we're proud of," says Sarah Hopkins, who's been a headteacher here for eight years. She says it doesn't tell the full story but admits "it is disappointing".

Welsh parents are currently thinking about the next steps for their children, with application deadlines for secondary school places at the end of this month. That comes at a time when the test results pose difficult questions about why Wales has so clearly underperformed relative to its closest neighbours. And with Wales's devolved government now run by a party other than Labour for the first time ever, can the new Plaid Cymru administration do what it's promised and improve standards?

Sarah Hopkins started teaching in 1998 - a year before the Welsh Assembly, now the Senedd, took over responsibility for education in Wales from Westminster.

In that time she's had to navigate many system-wide and school changes.

The latest challenge has been managing the big move from the old mishmash of 1960s-built classrooms to the vast new building.

But buildings alone do not drive excellence, and the gap between Wales and the other UK countries is getting wider.

Pisa (Programme for International Student Assessment) measures teenagers' skills in reading, maths and science. Sat by a sample of 15-year-olds – 3,406 in Wales in 2025, including some in Sarah Hopkins' school - it provides a snapshot of how education systems are performing.

On the day results were published, Wales' education Minister, Anna Brychan, euphemistically said they were "not where we want them to be". Others called them catastrophic.

The graphs are stark.

Wales first took part in the tests in 2006. There have been upticks along the way. But when the pandemic affected scores across the board in 2022, Wales fell back furthest. And the gulf grew in the latest results.

The OECD, the global economic development body which runs Pisa, says that 20 points equates to roughly a year of learning. That would mean Welsh 15-year-olds are about two years behind England's in reading, science and maths. In reading, they also trail teenagers in Scotland and Northern Ireland by a year.

Soon after the devolved administration was established, the Welsh Labour government of the early 2000s used its powers over education and other public services to go off on a different course to Tony Blair's Labour government at Westminster - creating what the then Welsh First Minister Rhodri Morgan called "clear, red water".

Secondary school league tables and standardised tests at seven, 11 and 14 (SATs) were scrapped. A new learning-through-play approach for the youngest pupils was an early flagship policy.

Poor Pisa results in 2010 brought about a drastic reappraisal. Plain speaking Education Minister Leighton Andrews called the results a "wake-up call" for a "complacent" system and introduced a new raft of reforms.

Alongside a literacy and numeracy drive, Andrews re-introduced accountability measures with annual reading and maths tests for seven-to-14 year olds, and a new school performance regime, called banding.

There were some parallels between the political styles of Andrews and the man in charge of England's schools system at the time, Conservative Michael Gove, who was on his own controversial education mission with an emphasis on high-stakes accountability. The two seemed to relish their occasional public spats over policy.

But policies introduced by Andrews lost their bite over time. The school banding system was changed and eventually dropped altogether during the pandemic. Tests later evolved into personalised assessments. And the focus moved to developing a new curriculum in Wales, something which Andrews recently said was a "distraction" from efforts to drive up standards.

Sir Nick Gibb, a former schools minister at Westminster who worked under Michael Gove, believes the main reason for Wales' Pisa woes is weak accountability.

He says "schools are spending billions of pounds of public money and they're not being held to account for the results that they produce".

He argues that focusing on the "science of learning" paid dividends with England's move up international education rankings. Primary schools in England were told they had to use a structured form of phonics to teach young children to read. This was reinforced with a phonics screening check for six-year-olds.

Sir Nick claims education standards in Wales and Scotland suffered because they didn't do the same.

In general, education ministers in England have been more likely to set direction for teachers, highlighted by the approach to phonics. In Wales, for the most part, the mantra has been to trust the profession. And though that freedom sounds good in theory, it has pitfalls.

It's the thinking at the heart of the new curriculum for Wales - dubbed the biggest reform to Welsh education in a generation.

There's widespread support for the core purposes of the curriculum which aim to create well-rounded young people with the skills to contribute to the economy and to society. But there's less confidence in the way it tries to go about achieving that.

The curriculum, which started being developed in 2014 and is only being fully rolled out this academic year, gives schools freedom to design their own curricula. In fact it's now "left almost completely up to schools what they should teach," says Lucy Crehan, an associate advisor on curriculum at Swansea University and education consultant.

Experts such as Crehan argue it's unlikely to improve standards and may make the situation worse by exacerbating inconsistency across schools.

And many teachers, already overstretched and overwhelmed, have struggled.

"I think there does need to be more clarity for teachers, for schools on what actually it is they should be teaching and where it is they should be getting students to and by what point," Crehan says. She warns that it is the most disadvantaged pupils who could come off worst.

"This is categorically not teachers' fault. They have been let down by a system that has said, you're the professionals, off you go and sort out everything", says Crehan.

There has been a growing consensus about the need to provide teachers with extra support, which was acknowledged by the previous Labour government. Teaching unions warn the profession is being asked to introduce the biggest reform to Welsh education in a generation while still dealing with the fallout of the pandemic, including poor attendance and behaviour, as well as squeezed budgets.

In the meantime, the real test of the curriculum's impact on standards is yet to come. The next Pisa tests, planned for 2029, will be the first with the new curriculum fully in place.

Apart from what's taught and how, there are other factors that could influence standards.

"There's nothing in the water in Wales that's different," says Nick Gibb. But, could the way the education system is structured play a part?

Unlike in England, in Wales there are no academies or free schools. Comprehensives, run by local authorities, are the norm. Former First Minister Lord Carwyn Jones believes that 22 councils is too many to run education effectively. He says failing to cut that number is his biggest regret in government.

Jones believes there is a "structural problem in Wales where the Welsh government sets policy…but doesn't deliver education", which is the job of local authorities.

Some councils oversee a handful of schools – including only four secondaries in some cases. "I just don't think you can have the right level of challenge or the right level of guidance if the local authority itself is very, very small," he says. Unless that's addressed, it's impossible "to provide the right level of support to improve our Pisa scores".

When Wales-based education economist Luke Sibieta compared GCSE results in areas such as Wrexham and Blaenau Gwent in Wales with the likes of similarly disadvantaged Gateshead and Salford in England, he found "disadvantaged pupils just perform worse in Wales than they do in England". The latest Pisa data showed the most disadvantaged pupils in England performed above the overall Welsh average in reading.

Taking the stage at Plaid Cymru's first conference in government, cabinet minister for Education Anna Brychan's assessment was more blunt than a month earlier, when the Pisa results came out. Speaking in Welsh, she called them "brawychus" - roughly translated as "terrible" or "shocking".

But so far she hasn't proposed wholesale changes to education. The minister has been at pains to emphasise that she's committed to the new curriculum. Even if it was practical to unpick it all, she's acknowledged there's little appetite for major upheaval. Instead, she's promising to review aspects of it and to set clearer steps for measuring how pupils are progressing.

Brychan's view is that a focus on literacy and numeracy has been "lost in the noise" of reforms. She's promised more clarity.

Phonics are more central to the plan and there will be more tracking of children's progress in primary school.

Wales' education system needs to be better at measuring itself, says Luke Sibieta, who is a research fellow at the Institute for Fiscal Studies. And without consistent benchmarks, it's not surprising that so much weight has been placed on Pisa's verdict. Sibieta makes the point that, looked at through a different lens, the downward trend in Wales' results is in line with "places like France, Germany, Italy, Spain" while England has been bucking the trend. That's little consolation for those involved in Welsh education.

Sarah Hopkins says her school has strived to build an effective curriculum due to professional pride and determination to make sure the "children get what they deserve", but she admits "there's no checks you're doing it properly".

Overall, she is optimistic that the new curriculum and efforts in schools to improve standards will bear fruit in better Pisa scores in future. "I think that there will be a time where Wales will lead the way," she says.

But some fear a generation of young people have been let down.

"It's not the be all and end all, how you do in Pisa," says Sibieta, "but if it means that young people are less highly skilled and less able to get good quality jobs later on in life, that has implications for all of us."

title: ‘This is the first time I’ve touched grass’: Inside the U.S. colleges pioneering social prescriptions
summary:

The post ‘This is the first time I’ve touched grass’: Inside the U.S. colleges pioneering social prescriptions  appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
This story is being published in partnership with MindSite News, a national news organization that reports on mental health and sends out a daily newsletter available here.

In 1984, while studying at Cornell University as a graduate student and going through a “difficult” time, Don Rakow remembers escaping to the campus gardens. “They were my sanctuaries—those gardens were essential for me to maintain balance and to survive,” he says.

Thirty years later, that moment came back to the English-major-turned-plant-science professor, when he began teaching at Cornell. As Rakow and fellow faculty members discussed what it would take to respond to the growing mental health crisis among students today, he suggested an unlikely candidate: their campus, and all of the natural wonders on it. What if Rakow could help struggling students find relief through green spaces, just like he did when he was in their shoes?

This experience led him to co-found NatureRx – one of the nation’s first dedicated programs designed to help students spend time engaging with nature as a way to improve their health. Today, in addition to operating as a student-run club that hosts nature-based activities, the program works with Cornell Health to support nature prescribing, through which on-campus physicians and counselors embed actual “referrals” for nature activities into students’ electronic health records – and then measure the results.

Dr. Jonathan Keffer, one of Cornell Health’s participating physicians, says the program helps students recognize how spending time in nature is more than just a nice-to-have. “This is actually physiologically proven medical treatment,” he explains, referencing the deep body of research demonstrating nature’s healing effects on stress, anxiety and depression.

Cornell’s NatureRx program is part of the growing movement for social prescribing — a practice through which a patient is referred to a non-medical, community-based activity, often involving nature, art, movement or service. Originating in the UK in the 1980s, social prescribing has been shown to boost patients’ health while reducing pressure and costs within health care.

Now, as more U.S. campuses struggle to keep up with demand for student mental health services, university-based social prescribing programs are cropping up around the country, from Michigan and California to New York and Arizona.

Rakow, who has since retired from Cornell, now co-directs the Campus Nature Rx Network, a separate LLC he co-founded in 2019 with professor Dorothy Ibes of the College of William & Mary, as a way to help universities build their own versions of the program. Funded through support from the REI Cooperative Action Fund and tuition from a sliding-scale certificate program, the network offers free membership and resources to schools starting their own nature prescribing programs. To date, about 120 colleges and universities have joined.

“There seems to be greater awareness that there need to be more tools for addressing student well-being,” Rakow says.

‘I feel lighter’

While U.S. colleges have existed for hundreds of years, it wasn’t until 1910 that any college created a dedicated mental health service — when Princeton University noticed students were dropping out because of emotional issues and hired a psychiatrist to address it. But a historical review suggests it took another four decades for campus counseling services to become mainstream, and another six before mental health care demand would exceed what campuses could provide.

Between 2009 and 2015, counseling center use grew much faster than student enrollment did, and the underlying need grew, too; one study of 350,000 students across 373 campuses between 2013 and 2021 found depression rose by 135 percent and anxiety by 110 percent. During that period, the number of students meeting the criteria for at least one mental health problem doubled.

In the early 2010s, a series of student suicides brought heightened attention to mental health and well-being at Cornell, prompting the university to expand its response efforts. In addition to hiring more counselors and training faculty in bystander intervention, Cornell supported Rakow to co-found NatureRx.

“Spending time in nature is not a cure-all,” Rakow notes, emphasizing the program’s intention isn’t to fully replace counseling or medication, but to complement other approaches to student well-being. A large body of research finds nature can help with some of the symptoms that counseling and medication can support — studies show that time outdoors can meaningfully reduce anxiety and depression. A Cornell-led study that Rakow co-authored even finds that mental health benefits can kick in after just 10 minutes outside.

Physiological studies show that time in nature helps reduce stress, which can often precede anxiety and depression by activating the body’s parasympathetic nervous system. This measurably reduces cortisol — the body’s primary stress hormone.

This link between nature and stress reduction matters at a university like Cornell, where many students not only experience intense academic pressures, but also a stressful sociopolitical climate, says Rakow. “Concerns about climate change, the economy, loss of women’s rights and democratic rights, pressures brought upon by social media — there’s (a) long list.”

While flyers and campus maps of nature hotspots on and around campus can help students “self-prescribe” nature, many learn about NatureRx through their doctor or counselor. In practice, the process typically begins with a gentle conversation from a health professional, when a student seeks treatment for anxiety, depression, or sometimes “a physical complaint that has a substantial undercurrent of mental health,” says Dr. Kent Bullis, a physician from Cornell Health.

A student might come in for insomnia, for instance, “with difficulty sleeping and fatigue,” Bullis says, “and oftentimes, when you explore that in depth, it becomes obvious that stress is playing a role.” In those cases, he is careful about how he raises NatureRx: “I try to plant the seed that this could be related to stress without making them feel like I’m dismissing their symptoms entirely.”

Keffer, his Cornell Health colleague, similarly tries to offer a scientific explanation of the ways nature can help address certain symptoms. “I may medicalize it a little bit — talk about the vagal tone, (how nature) cools down the nervous system — to make it seem more like a treatment,” he says. Especially when prescribing nature alongside antidepressants, he says he “tries to weave it into the treatment plan,”explaining that nature “can modulate your anxiety response, counter your sympathetic nervous system and enhance your more relaxing parasympathetic nervous system.”

From there, after physicians check a box in patients’ electronic health records to indicate NatureRx was discussed, students are encouraged to create their own nature prescription, whether that’s joining a nature excursion club or simply choosing to study outside. “We have a little card that providers can give out to help students make their own nature plan … and we give specific examples because some of our students are less familiar with what to do outside,” explains Emily Dunuwila, the health initiatives coordinator within Cornell’s NatureRx program.

Some of the most popular and reliable options — hosted all year long, even through the campus’ dark and cold winters — have been the student clubs. Since the program’s founding, there’s been the NatureRx club — an undergraduate-run group hosting indoor crafting sessions, outdoor bingo walks, and interactive discussions on topics like climate anxiety and the science of awe.

Today, Big Red Barn Guided Nature Walks — led by students — take place on Wednesdays, rain-or-shine, with ponchos provided. Sofia Mattson, a master’s student in design and environmental analysis, founded the walking group after realizing that students were hardly noticing their campus’ unique natural wonders — from the waterfalls and gorges to the botanic gardens. “As a student, you only go to a couple locations a day, and generally, the only reason you’re outside is to get from one place to the next,” she says.

To break that pattern and encourage students to be more perceptive, Mattson encourages walkers to engage with their natural surroundings using all five senses. She invites them to find what she calls their “nature ally” — a squirrel, a rock, a bit of lavender sage or even a cherry from a cherry tree — and then to see, hear, touch, smell and sometimes even taste their way through it.

“After the walk, you can tell it really made a difference because people kind of stick around and talk to each other about life and say, ‘Wow, that was really nice, and it was so great to get out here,’” Mattson says.

Despite the formality of the prescribing process and availability of options, NatureRx is careful not to overwhelm students with an inflexible prescription. “It’s really customizable — it’s not necessarily ‘Join this group, join this thing’… it’s more of, let’s see how we can integrate this into your busy schedule in a way that works for you,” explains Dunuwila, the program’s coordinator.

And though that variability makes it hard to measure the program’s precise impact — some students may spend five minutes a day, while others may spend several hours per week — the data paints a promising picture: In 2024-2025, Cornell Health providers prescribed or recommended time in nature to more than 2,200 students, and according to responses from surveys sent to students who received a nature prescription, 88 percent reported an improvement in mood and 85 percent reported that they felt less stressed.

Though the survey results capture a small and potentially skewed picture of the program (only 30 percent of students who received the survey completed it), the physicians’ observations track with its positive results: The doctors said they’ve seen meaningful clinical improvements in the mental health of students they’ve given prescriptions to, as well as in their productivity and time management.

“When students got back to the work (after their nature prescription), they told me they felt more clear, more receptive,” says Keffer. He says he now frames NatureRx as not only as a mental health tool but also as an academic one, particularly for the many students who think they don’t have time for nature, he says. “It’s actually very impactful on decreasing procrastination — it can be looked at as a time saver, an investment.”

The student leaders also witnessed powerful transformations in their peers. In the NatureRx club, co-president Arianna Sprenger remembers the afternoon she led a club walk through the arboretum, when a fellow student shared out loud, “I feel so much lighter.” And for Mattson, she remembers a simple aha moment from one student who joined her Big Red Barn walk. “I have literally been on my laptop for hours today,” the student said. “This is the first time I’ve actually touched grass.”

‘All of my worries disappear’

Outside of Cornell and the 100-plus other campuses in the Campus Nature Rx network, some universities are designing their own social prescribing programs, as new data shines light on the need: According to the 2024-25 Healthy Minds Study, which surveyed more than 84,000 students across 135 colleges and universities, 37 percent of students reported moderate to severe depressive symptoms, and nearly 1 in 4 reported often feeling isolated from others. Meanwhile, according to a survey of more than 130 U.S. campus counseling leaders conducted by Timely Care, a provider of virtual mental health services to campus counseling centers, 86 percent of counselors say student mental health needs are increasing.

To help meet students’ mental health needs outside of clinical care, campuses like University of Arizona and Stanford University are partnering with SocialRx (formerly Art Pharmacy), an Atlanta-based, for-profit company that connects patients to community activities to improve their mental health. At Stanford, a network of campus organizations — from student affairs to athletics — refer students to a dedicated SocialRx care navigator, who learns about each student’s interests, challenges and schedule and can then prescribe up to nine “doses” of arts and cultural experiences. Those experiences could include everything from museum visits and dance workshops to pottery classes and live performances, all at no cost to the student.

The early results at Stanford are encouraging; according to data from SocialRx, 84 percent of referred students attended the activities, and 80 percent of those students reported improved mental health. Deborah Cullinan, vice president for the arts at Stanford University, says the arts and cultural partners providing the activities are equally enthusiastic.

“We thought we’d get about a half-dozen partners, but I think we now have 40,” she explains. “It wasn’t just us making the case that arts would be an important tool in the toolkit to support students — it really started to be the case that people are calling us.”

Some skeptics may wonder why social prescribing is necessary on college campuses, which typically are rife with social activities already. Lindsey Mortenson, a clinical assistant professor of psychiatry and chief mental health officer of student life at the University of Michigan, says that paradox puzzled her, too. “We started from a place of concern and curiosity about students’ loneliness and disconnection, because the problem that we have at Michigan is definitely not lack of opportunity … there’s no shortage of arts events almost every day on campus.”

To get a clearer picture of students’ loneliness, Mortenson and her colleagues ran a sample survey — posting QR codes across dining halls, housing, and student unions to understand why students weren’t showing up to existing activities.

“The number one barrier students cited was time,” Mortenson says, summarizing the 1,400 student survey responses. “But there was also this other factor — a lot of social anxiety, lacking social skills and social confidence.”

That survey, albeit informal, recently helped to catalyze two formal social prescribing efforts at Michigan. One is a student program, Experience Rx, which will actively prescribe students activities involving art, nature, movement, shared meals, and community service, making it one of the first comprehensive campus social prescribing programs in the country. The other is a research arm, the Institute for Social Prescribing, which will study the impact of ExperienceRx and other campus social prescribing programs.

“A lot of [students] are like, 70 percent of the way there — they just need someone to help them take that last step,” says Mortenson, who is now co-director of the institute.

As Michigan seeks to understand the research impact of campus social prescribing programs, other universities are taking a more grassroots approach. At the University of Oregon, teaching professor Lisa Abia-Smith leads what might be the nation’s first dedicated undergraduate course on social prescribing, in which students are invited to design their own programs and reflect on the concept.

At New York University, David Hollander, an assistant dean and clinical professor, teaches a course called “How Basketball Can Save the World.” Through the course, students are taught about the ways basketball — with its components of movement, service and belonging — can serve as a social prescription. Then, they’re invited to lead a campaign promoting HoopsRx — a program connecting middle school students dealing with anxiety and loneliness to free, structured recreational basketball.

This past spring, Ani Minic, a sophomore studying sports management who also plays for Montenegro’s women’s national soccer team, was one of more than 100 students who spent an afternoon blanketing park benches and lamp posts with HoopsRx flyers. “Before you knew it, there were probably 1,000 plus flyers all around the city,” she says, with each one reading: “HoopsRx. It’s better than aspirin.”

For Minic, the campaign was more than a class assignment; it took her back to a revelation she made in childhood and which she recalled when she recently stumbled across her old journal. “A lot of people say their ‘happy place’ is at a beach or somewhere peaceful and relaxed,” she read, quoting her 12-year-old self. “However, my happy place is on the fields … I step on the field, and all of my worries disappear.”

This article was supported by The Carter Center for Mental Health Reporting. The writer, Julia Hotz, is a 2025-2026 Carter Center Mental Health Fellow.

title: Survey: Majority of College Students Say Free Speech Threatened
summary:
Survey: Majority of College Students Say Free Speech Threatened
kathryn.palmer… Wed, 10/14/2026 - 03:00 AM

Just 37 percent of college students said free speech feels secure, compared to 73 percent in 2016.

Byline(s)
Kathryn Palmer
full_text:
A record share of college students believe their right to free speech is under threat, new data shows.

Just 37 percent of college students said free speech is secure, compared to 73 percent in 2016, according to a survey of more than 1,000 college students that the Knight Foundation released Tuesday in partnership with Ipsos.

“That’s the lowest level that’s ever been observed,” said Ricardo Mor, program officer for the Knight Foundation’s information and society team. “It’s an alarming trend.”

Since 2016, when the survey was first conducted, college students have lost confidence that their other freedoms—including to practice religion, petition the government and peacefully assemble—are secure. For example, only 40 percent of college students now believe that their right to a free press is secure, compared to 81 percent a decade ago.

The findings come amid ongoing debates over free expression and academic freedom on campus. The past 10 years have been marked by instances of students shouting down speakers with opposing political views, universities punishing pro-Palestinian campus activists and lawmakers dictating what faculty can teach and research.

However, 57 percent of college students surveyed this year said the climate on their campus discouraged them to speak their mind, the lowest level since 2016. While that’s an improvement since 2021—when a record 65 percent of college students said they felt uncomfortable sharing their views—“it’s really hard to make definitive judgments” from these data alone, said John Sands, vice president of the Knight Foundation’s information and society team.

“Surveys measure a moment in time, and given the volume of things that have happened in the past several years, especially on college campuses, it’s hard to know what students are responding to,” he said. “It could be broader societal trends or flare-ups of speech issues on specific campuses.”

Conducted last spring, the college student survey is one part of the latest Knight Foundation–Ipsos Future of the First Amendment study, which examined attitudes toward free speech among 18- to 29-year-olds regardless of their education status. Similar to the college student subgroup, it found that 65 percent of young people believe their freedom of speech is under threat.

Even if it feels tenuous, young people—including college students—still value free speech. According to the survey, 84 percent of college students said it’s either extremely or very important.

At the same time, college students are increasingly interested in their institutions protecting them from speech perceived as biased or offensive. Forty-six percent of survey respondents this year (the highest number on record) said colleges should “allow students to be exposed to all types of speech,” compared to 82 percent in 2017. Meanwhile, 28 percent of students said colleges should protect them by prohibiting potentially offensive speech, compared to 18 percent in 2017.

College students’ attitudes about the state of free expression on campus also vary depending on factors such as their political affiliation and race.

About 27 percent of Democrats this year said their freedom of speech felt secure, compared to 59 percent of Republicans. But when Democrats controlled the White House, responses were flipped. In 2024, just 34 percent of Republican college students said free speech was secure, compared to 51 percent of Democrats. In addition, Black students this year said it is difficult to express themselves on campus without consequence, while white students said it’s relatively easy.

Although the survey doesn’t draw any conclusions about what’s driving these trends, Sands said the findings can inform the development of the civil discourse programs that have become popular on college campuses.

“It’s a hot topic at the moment. Campus administrators are trying to figure out how to make their campuses places where tough dialogue can happen and ideas can be debated,” he said. “These data are a national baseline for how college students are feeling about speech issues. It’s a starting point to begin thinking about what you can do on your campus and what sort of interventions can help move the needle at the local level.”

title: 5 Colleges Sign On as Founding Members of New Accreditor
summary:
5 Colleges Sign On as Founding Members of New Accreditor
Katherine Knott Wed, 10/14/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Katherine Knott
full_text:
Five independent colleges said Tuesday that they are joining the National Association for Academic Excellence, a new accreditor, as founding members.

Leaders from Bellevue University, Benedictine College, Houston Christian University, Merrimack College in Massachusetts and the University of Mount Saint Vincent will serve on NAAE’s board and help to refine the association’s accreditation standards.

Launched in 2024, NAAE says it’s designed specifically for independent colleges and universities with standards focused on student achievement, education value and the “formation of the whole person,” according to the release. NAAE also noted that its standards will respect “each institution’s autonomy to define and pursue its distinctive mission as it meets the changing needs of students and society.”

NAAE CEO Rob Manzer said in the release that by signing up as founding members, the five colleges have demonstrated confidence in the association’s mission and vision.

“Their commitment reﬂects a shared belief that accreditation can and should do more to advance academic excellence, protect institutional independence, and strengthen accountability to students and the public,” he said.

The association is among several aspiring accreditors that plan to seek federal recognition in coming years. Until then, the founding members will stick with their current accreditors, according to the release. Colleges must be accredited by a federally recognized agency in order to access federal student aid. The Trump administration is currently working to finalize a rule that would make it easier for new accreditors to gain federal recognition.

Seven institutional accreditors oversee most colleges and universities, but NAAE argues that “serving that range of institutions made it difficult to consistently apply standards and uphold academic rigor.”

Susan Burns, president of the University of Mount Saint Vincent, said in the release that she and the other founding members are helping to build an accreditor “that will uphold academic excellence, recognize the value of different approaches and keep student success at the center of the process.”

Burns, Merrimack College President Christopher Hopey and others noted that independent colleges are a diverse group, and they hope NAAE will recognize their missions and give them freedom to innovate.

Stephen Minnis, president of Benedictine College, a Catholic institution in Kansas, noted that independent colleges “make their greatest contribution when they are free to follow their missions in an unimpeded manner.”

“We are excited to help build an accreditor that will demand the highest standards of academic excellence while allowing faith-based institutions to form students in accordance with their faith traditions,” Minnis added.

title: Expanding College Success for Low-Income Students
summary:
Expanding College Success for Low-Income Students
Joshua.Bay Wed, 10/14/2026 - 03:00 AM

A $42 million gift from MacKenzie Scott aims to help the nonprofit 10,000 Degrees scale its student support model and expand college completion efforts by 2031.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
An unrestricted $42 million gift from philanthropist MacKenzie Scott and Yield Giving is helping 10,000 Degrees, a nonprofit dedicated to supporting students from low-income backgrounds, significantly expand its reach and help more students earn diplomas.

The donation, the largest in the organization’s history, will fund efforts outlined in a new five-year strategic plan aimed at delivering its programs to new communities, doubling the annual number of college students it supports from 5,000 to 10,000 and improving college completion and career outcomes. Under the plan, which spans fiscal years 2027 through 2031, the nonprofit seeks to raise the four-year community college transfer rate from 44 percent to 60 percent and increase the six-year bachelor’s degree–attainment rate among transfer students from 53 percent to 70 percent. It also hopes to increase the share of college students engaged in career success programming from 30 percent to 80 percent.

Kim Mazzuca, president and chief executive officer of 10,000 Degrees, said the gift does not change the organization’s strategic direction or priorities but instead allows it to make up-front investments to accelerate existing initiatives.

“We need more students to move through their education and land meaningful careers so they can go back into their communities and make positive change,” Mazzuca said. “So much weighs on education. That is the most important lever that we can pull right now, and Mackenzie Scott knew that, so we are going to make the absolute most of her gift and this strategic plan.”

A five-year road map: Scott’s donation to 10,000 Degrees is one of a series of major philanthropic investments she has made in organizations and institutions geared toward historically underserved students. In recent years, she has also awarded $50 million to the Native Forward Scholars Fund, $70 million to the United Negro College Fund and $63 million to Morgan State University.

For 10,000 Degrees, the investment will help advance the nonprofit’s strategic priorities, intended to strengthen its college success model and support its long-term growth.

The plan calls for expanding scholarships and college-readiness programs, as well as community college transfer support and career guidance. Mazzuca said affordability remains a significant barrier for community college students, many of whom balance their education with employment and family responsibilities. In the past fiscal year, the nonprofit helped students secure more than $70 million in additional financial aid.

“For some of our students, starting at a community college is just more affordable for themselves and their family,” Mazzuca said. “Many of our community college students stay close to home because they’re not only working but they’re also helping to support their families and the household income.”

The plan also outlines efforts to integrate technology and artificial intelligence into student services, including predictive analytics, real-time data and digital tools designed to improve personalized support.

“What AI is going to help us do is to actually be able to suss out the priority students that need certain levels of intervention,” Mazzuca said. “Then we can lean out where students don’t need us as much, and we can lean out from the administrative aspects of tracking students and inputting data.”

Other priorities include expanding the organization’s state and national policy influence through partnerships, advocacy and sharing effective practices with higher education networks. The plan also emphasizes strengthening organizational capacity through investments in systems, near-peer mentoring and operational efficiency, even as it works to ensure long-term financial sustainability by diversifying funding and strengthening its financial reserves.

Mazzuca said partnerships with existing college-access programs will be particularly important to the organization’s expansion, allowing 10,000 Degrees to build on established services while providing additional financial and academic support to help students persist and graduate.

“What we want to be able to do is to develop partnerships with those access programs and say, ‘Let us come in and augment the good work that you’re already doing,’” Mazzuca said.

Beyond college completion: The organization currently reports an 80 percent graduation rate among its four-year college students; of those, 85 percent graduate debt-free. Its strategic plan aims to build on those outcomes while placing greater emphasis on career preparation to help ensure students not only graduate but also transition into meaningful careers.

“There are fast-changing forces right now within workforce development and labor markets, given this huge disruption with AI,” Mazzuca said, adding that the students the nonprofit serves “have incredible talent, are innovators and have incredible dreams and hopes, but don’t have the social networks.”

“We want to make sure that our students, by the time they graduate, have already developed or are already in the midst of developing their social capital,” she added.

The expansion also comes at a time when questions about the value of a college degree have become increasingly prominent, Mazzuca noted.

“The rhetoric about ‘Is college worth it?’ is, to me, absurd when we know that a college degree is the absolute surest pathway to both social and economic mobility,” she said. “A college degree is critically important, especially for our students coming from low-income backgrounds. It is what is going to change their lives forever in terms of mobility and living a healthy, happy and prosperous life.”

title: The Odd Couple: The Differences Between Colleges and Universities
summary:
The Odd Couple: The Differences Between Colleges and Universities
rachel.toor Wed, 10/14/2026 - 03:00 AM

Rachel and Gordon go to a small college campus and Gordon learns how much he didn’t know.

Byline(s)
Rachel Toor
E. Gordon Gee
full_text:
RST: Since we started doing this column nine months ago (!), you’ve wanted us to take our show on the road. I said, “No way, minion.” I like to sit behind my computer at home, and we all know I write better than I talk. You are a showman and it’s terrifying to share a stage with you. But we just had our debut at Hendrix College. Thoughts?

EGG: Well, first I am just recovering from my Valium stupor after you nearly killed us driving in the roundabouts in Conway, Ark. As we continue our travels, we are definitely using Uber. As for Hendrix, it was absolutely everything you told me to expect: small campus looking like a movie set; leadership that is transparent and admired for being so; a faculty that either were lying or actually did expect to be responsible stewards in a shared governance system; students and staff exuding unusual commitment to the cause; a Board of Trustees that were devoted to the success of the president and supportive of her leadership. It was unexpected and awesome.

RST: We decided we would never charge institutions who want to host our wacky Odd Couple performance, but I think we have to agree that there will be no more renting of cars. Those goddamn roundabouts. My driving scared both of us.

EGG: Well, thanks for fessing up that you nearly killed us. Let’s just admit that we are both incapable of taking care of ourselves without outside intervention.

RST: Adulting is hard. I’ve been saying higher ed is a gorgeous mosaic and have been ragging on you for only seeing the giant tiles. I’ve slowly been trying to teach you, Grasshopper, about the other 99 percent by introducing you to leaders of different types of institutions. You’ve been wowed by them, but this was your first chance to spend time on a campus unlike those you’ve been accustomed to for the past century. What did you learn at Hendrix that surprised you?

EGG: I could say so much, but I want to be succinct: I was blown away by the clear-eyed focus of President Karen Petersen and the board because they realize they have no room for error. At big institutions, even though there are massive challenges, kicking the ball down the field and having one more round of planning is the modus operandi, because they have longer runways. At Hendrix, with 1,000 students and 100 faculty, every student counts on the bottom line. There’s no room for delay or mistakes. I would have hives and never sleep with that Damocles sword over my head.

RST: It was hilarious when we had dinner with Karen and you said, in a totally ingenuous way, “You actually have to run this place!” O brave new world! When we talk about general issues in higher education, we tend to agree more than we disagree. But in our conversation with the board, each time we were asked a question, you would go first (from your throne) and provide an answer that was smart, funny and dead wrong. When it was my turn, I’d have to say, “Jane, you ignorant slut!” Fortunately, most of the trustees were old enough to get the SNL reference and laugh at the joke.

EGG: Everyone laughed but me.🤓 This is my learning curve and one of the many reasons I am glad to join you on this journey. I have always understood the power and poetry of the small institutions, but I have, much to my detriment, never fully comprehended their unique challenges. I thought that there would be learnings that I could pass along to the folks at Hendrix; I will now admit that some of my observations were totally inapplicable to this institution. Of course you had to immediately correct me, and to my chagrin they seemed to resonate more with you than me. And you have no fear of disagreeing, which is our compact: Agree, disagree or find common ground, but be very open and honest. It is a rolling seminar.

RST: For better or worse, we can only be ourselves. Though I did make a sign that I held up in one of our meetings that read “Why we can’t all be Gordon Gee.” Everyone laughed—except you. When the president introduced us, she told the board she had no idea what we were going to say. I think we surprised each other. We continue to learn from our partnership and to have a lot of fun while doing it. Everyone told me they appreciated our different perspectives and saw how much real affection we have for each other. Did I say anything you vehemently disagree with?

EGG: I did not disagree (because I was scared)! Truthfully, I thought your comments spoke more directly to the board and administration than mine. Through The Sandbox and being so nosy, you have gained a perspective which speaks to a vast number of institutions that are seeking help. I do not believe that I was necessarily wrong, but I was not sector-specific. Lesson learned. What is good for the goose may not be good for the gander.

RST: I saw no geese, but before you arrived I did go for a run and tried to talk to a bunch of turtles. Walking on campus with you, we were late for everything because you cannot simply pass by anyone without saying hello and finding out their entire life story, from the student who drove us around in a golf cart to the women’s softball coach to the dining hall workers. You ask questions, pay attention and remember things about people. It’s genuine and everyone freaking loves you. Still, we were late for everything and I hate being late.

EGG: It is irritating to everyone with whom I work, because I am unable to just meet a schedule. I love the energy of a place and I want to hear from those who are living and learning on a campus. And I hate meetings because they waste time and energy and are not “doing.” The more you formally meet, the less you accomplish. Try that on for a mantra!

RST: After dinner, you gave a terrific talk to the trustees about their role. That’s where you brought the Gee magic.

EGG: It became clear that Hendrix is at an inflection point and everyone on the board must commit their time and treasure to ensuring that they meet and exceed their fundraising goal and that they have a consistent message about Hendrix. They cannot afford a cacophony of voices or half-hearted engagement. They have done the hard lifting in rightsizing the institution and stopping the financial bleeding, but now they have no choice but to be fully engaged in the process of change.

RST: You missed the SNL joke because, as one of the trustees pointed out, you were too busy working in those days to watch TV. At Hendrix, you showed up with a BELIEVE lapel pin, channeling Ted Lasso.

EGG: I did. I love the humor and wisdom of that show. And I think it speaks to the times. I know this sounds a bit naïve but we must believe in the possibilities of education, including higher education, and not let the cynical hysteria start to define us. That, by the way, is also something that I did learn from Hendrix—in a small town in Arkansas, on a small campus, that people are believing in the work they are doing.

RST: You were there only for one day, but I stayed on for the board meeting and talked to students, faculty and their amazing career services team. I asked everyone I met if they’d seen season two of A Man on the Inside. Karen Petersen had told me a while ago that Mary Steenburgen had gone to Hendrix and that her experience provided inspiration for fictional Wheeler College. It’s about a $400 million donation from a billionaire whose agenda involves a hostile corporate-style takeover to, oh, let’s see, restructure and gut the college. Hilarity ensues. Ted Danson’s character is repeatedly asked the question posed to all new students: “Francis Wheeler came here in search of gold, but he found something much more important. What did Wheeler find?”

As corny as it is, I found the same thing at Hendrix. Now you have to watch the series to learn the answer, but it won’t surprise you.

title: Restoring nature is key to a more resilient future
summary: At COP17 and COP31, governments must accelerate positive tipping points in energy, food and finance.
full_text:
Nature is humanity’s life-support system, but it is being depleted at an alarming rate, leaving our world increasingly vulnerable. From deadly heatwaves and raging wildfires to catastrophic floods and prolonged droughts, the effects of environmental change have been impossible to ignore this year. With El Nino forecast to intensify, the risks to people, nature and economies are only increasing.

These shocks are unfolding against the backdrop of widespread nature loss, with WWF’s Living Planet Report 2026 finding that the average size of monitored wildlife populations declined by 73 percent between 1970 and 2022. Nature loss is increasingly a question of economic and national resilience – affecting food and water security, health, supply chains and geopolitical stability.

The situation is serious, but science shows there are still grounds for hope.

The economic systems driving nature’s decline can be transformed, and change can accelerate much faster than many may expect. Evidence shows that under the right conditions, positive change can cross a tipping point threshold and become self-reinforcing, making a safer, more resilient future not just possible, but inevitable.

The question is: How can we accelerate the actions needed to trigger those tipping points and accelerate the transition?

Positive tipping points and the opportunity for transformational change

In environmental terms, we often think about tipping points in terms of the threats they pose to vital ecosystems, such as coral reefs or the Amazon rainforest, where constant damage risks compounding and becoming increasingly impossible to reverse. These dangers are real and urgent. However, these tipping point dynamics can also work in our favour.

Three economic systems are driving most of nature’s decline: the energy system that fuels climate change; the global food system that leads to habitat loss and climate change; and the finance system that bankrolls it all. Triggering tipping points in those systems would see them rapidly transform for the better and reduce harm to the climate and nature. Once that threshold is passed, change can happen quickly as knowledge and technology advance, with solutions becoming cheaper and more accessible and as people learn from others. Encouragingly, progress is already under way – not everywhere, and not yet at the scale required – but enough to demonstrate that change is possible.

The world does not lack goals for 2030. What it lacks is the pace of implementation. With the Global Biodiversity Framework, the UN Sustainable Development Goals and the Paris Agreement in place, governments have already agreed on a pathway. Focusing on implementing these agreements in full will create the conditions for rapid systemic change.

The global energy system has already passed a tipping point, with the transition away from fossil fuels to renewable energy now accelerating. While far from complete, this transition demonstrates how rapid systemic change is possible, offering valuable lessons for the equally urgent transformation of our food and financial systems.

Twenty years ago, solar power was used mostly in satellites and pocket calculators. Now, it is the cheapest option for new electricity generation in most countries. Affordable solar panels are electrifying rural households and improving the resilience of food and medical supply chains. Renewable technologies are displacing fossil fuels at a pace few people predicted even a decade ago.

Changing the food and finance systems is proving slower but is no less urgent.

To progress towards a food systems tipping point, we need to hit major milestones in the uptake of nature-positive food production and see wider shifts in consumer demand for healthier, more sustainable foods to reinforce and reward this shift. Some progress is under way with efforts to tackle commodity-driven deforestation, and more than 130 countries have national strategic plans for food system transformation, but commitments have not yet translated into the policies and incentives needed to accelerate the transition.

Tipping the finance system so that more finance flows to activities that protect and restore nature than activities that harm it is a fundamental challenge. Reaching this tipping point will require a combination of regulatory change, subsidy reform, and a shift in how the sector values climate and nature as material financial risks. If even a portion of the money currently directed towards harmful activities is redirected to environmental recovery, it could shift the economics of the entire transformation.

Governments meeting at the COP17 biodiversity and COP31 climate conferences have before them a vital opportunity to work together to accelerate the actions needed to trigger positive tipping points and to build resilience into societies and the global economy.

Learning from conservation success

Hidden within the broader picture of global biodiversity decline are inspiring stories of species recovery. Populations of green sea turtles and tigers are rebounding due to dedicated conservation work bringing together governments, communities and organisations.

Creating systemic change will similarly take action from all of us, from governments to businesses, financial institutions, local communities, and individuals. We know where we need to get to and the hurdles we need to overcome together; the task now is to create the conditions in which positive change gathers momentum and starts reinforcing itself.

Building strength and resilience into our natural support system will require the courage to shift from extractive, wasteful economies focused on short-term gain to systems that are sustainable and regenerative for the long-term benefit of all. We have the goals, the solutions and pathways to get there. Yes, there might be setbacks along the way, but science shows nature and the climate can still recover and that change can happen faster than we might think.

title: Universities warn funding gap leaves sector at cliff-edge
summary: Universities are to tell an Oireachtas committee that they are at capacity and teetering on a cliff-edge unless the Government addresses a funding gap in higher education.
full_text:
Universities are to tell an Oireachtas committee that they are at capacity and teetering on a cliff-edge unless the Government addresses a funding gap in higher education.

The head of the Irish Universities Association (IUA), which represents seven universities, will be joined by representatives of Trinity College Dublin, University College Dublin and University College Cork, at the Oireachtas Committee on Further and Higher Education later today.

The group had sought €190 million in additional core funding in Budget 2027 but €10m in additional funding was ultimately provided in last week's announcement.

IUA Director General Paul Johnston will tell TDs and Senators how third-level education is underfunded by €250m annually.

In 2022, a Government commissioned report identified a €307 million funding gap at third-level.

"Five budgets later, the original deficit is down to around €130 million. But as we know in our own lives, household costs don't stand still as you pay down your mortgage. Unfunded pay costs and unfunded growth in student numbers have pushed the real gap above €250 million per annum", Mr Johnston will state in his opening address.

"Ireland is one of the world’s most highly educated societies. The choice is whether to allow that to erode or to put our university sector on a sustainable footing", he will warn.

Chair of UCD's Governing Authority Mike Beary will stipulate how the institution "is now at the absolute limit of capacity - resourcefulness can’t substitute for a properly funded system."

"It is incumbent upon us to point to the very real cliff-edge we are teetering upon," Paul Farrell, Chairperson of the Board of Trinity College Dublin, will say in his opening statement.

"The harsh reality is that State funding per student is now over 30% lower in real terms than in 2008. This country ranks 36th out of 37 OECD countries for investment in higher education as a share of GDP," he will say.

In a briefing document to TDs and Senators, University College Cork claims the status quo represents a threat to the financial sustainability of the institution and raises doubts over its capacity to "maintain and renew its estate and research infrastructure".

It also says underfunding represents a "threat to essential capital investment", leads to a "deterioration of the student experience", and reduces the "ability to attract and retain talent".

Chair of UCC's Governing Authority Sean O’Driscoll will tell the committee that "UCC has become increasingly reliant on non-Exchequer income, philanthropy, international student recruitment and commercial income".

"From a governance perspective, our concern is the growing misalignment between national ambitions for higher education and the resources available to realise them", he will say.

He will also claim that UCC contributes €1.2 billion annually to the economy and supports 21,000 jobs across Cork and the wider southwest.

"While student numbers have increased by 23% over the last eight years, core state funding, adjusted for inflation, has only increased by €28m over the same period", he will say.

In its pre-budget submission to Minister for Further and Higher Education James Lawless, the IUA has also sought €250m over five years in capital spending to upgrade universities’ digital infrastructure "to provide teaching and research at the cutting edge of AI".

It also wanted €475m over four years in capital spending to create fully sustainable campuses.

Both Mr Lawless and the Minister of State for Higher Education Marian Harkin have defended Government investment in the sector.

Mr Lawless also last week secured a €150 universal cut in the student contribution charge which has been welcomed by university leaders.

title: Ireland’s international education challenge is access, not demand
summary:
As visa uncertainty clouds a growing sector, Irish education leaders warn that bureaucracy and inconsistent decisions could weaken the country’s appeal to global students.

The post Ireland’s international education challenge is access, not demand appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Ireland’s international education sector has a clear selling point, with demand remaining strong. But panellists at The PIE Live Ireland said the challenge is ensuring students can get through the door.

“Ireland’s overall numbers are still strong. So it’s not an issue of demand, it’s an issue of access,” said Lorcan O’Connor Lloyd, CEO of English Education Ireland.

That access is increasingly shaped by visa processing, refusal decisions and uncertainty over future policy. For a country that has built its international student appeal on openness and stability, the panel warned, inconsistency could quickly become a competitive disadvantage.

“Our message to government is: of course, you have to operate a fair and vast immigration system, but don’t let bureaucracy get in the way of talent. Please continue to make sure that international students are able to compete in a timely way,” said Paul Johnston, director general of the Irish Universities Association (IUA), describing international education as vital not only to universities but to Ireland’s wider economy and global connections.

Don’t let bureaucracy get in the way of talent. Please continue to make sure that international students are able to compete in a timely way

Paul Johnston, Irish Universities Association

The concern is that delays or unclear requirements could deter students before they arrive. Johnston said the sector had sought explanations after a rise in visa refusals for applicants from Gaza, noting that four students challenged refusals in court, with three challenges successful.

For Johnston, the broader stakes go beyond recruitment, as Ireland will need international talent to meet future workforce needs. The country’s universities want to keep channels open for the “investors and the designers and innovators of tomorrow”.

The issue is not, panellists stressed, whether Ireland should operate an immigration system with proper checks. It is whether the process is predictable, timely and clear to applicants.

Declan Coogan, associate director of student recruitment at Trinity College Dublin, said visa uncertainty complicates institutions’ long-term planning. “We are assuming that what we’re seeing in other countries is probably coming here in some form,” he said, describing how recruiters are building resilience while trying not to miss emerging markets.

Coogan said Ireland’s reputation for stability has helped attract students and partners, but that advantage is not guaranteed. “If we don’t … get some kind of consistency and alignment about our visa policy,” he warned, Ireland could miss opportunities in a changing global market.

Trinity has been broadening its recruitment base, with a 53% increase in American postgraduate students over the past two years, said Coogan. The university has also seen traction in Europe, while identifying potential for deeper engagement with regions including Africa and Latin America.

For English language education, visa access is already reflected in recruitment patterns. O’Connor Lloyd said visa-free markets – including Brazil, Chile, Argentina, Mexico, Japan and South Korea – are important to the sector. Ireland has remained comparatively resilient as the global English language teaching market has contracted, aided by a shift towards young learners and EU students.

“It’s not an issue of demand; it’s an issue of access,” he said.

Mary Grennan, head of international education at Quality and Qualifications Ireland (QQI), said that unanticipated immigration-policy changes could create significant difficulties for providers and representative bodies trying to plan. Alongside predictable access, she pointed to the role of quality assurance in maintaining confidence in Ireland’s offer.

title: Filiera bufalina, plafond di 30 milioni per le imprese della Piana del Sele
summary: L’uso di nuove tecnologie per la sostenibilità può dare slancio alla filiera bufalina della Piana del Sele, nel Salernitano. È la tesi alla base del progetto promosso da Fondazione Symbola...
full_text:
L’uso di nuove tecnologie per la sostenibilità può dare slancio alla filiera bufalina della Piana del Sele, nel Salernitano. full_text:
Un mese di scuola, e nemmeno un giorno libero da riunioni, moduli, circolari e decine di email. La professione è svuotata dall’interno, il tempo per preparare, studiare e seguire gli studenti viene divorato dalla burocrazia. È una trasformazione lenta ma costante: il mestiere conserva il nome di insegnamento, mentre una parte sempre più grande di tempo ed energie se ne va in tutto ciò che gli gira intorno.

È passato un mese dall’inizio della scuola e non c’è stato un giorno, uno soltanto, senza riunioni pomeridiane, moduli da compilare, form da riempire, scadenze da rispettare, circolari da leggere e decine/ventine/trentine di email istituzionali che reclamano attenzione, possibilmente immediata. Almeno venti messaggi al giorno sembrano ormai una misura ordinaria, come se la posta elettronica fosse diventata il registro di una reperibilità permanente e il tempo degli insegnanti una risorsa pubblica alla quale attingere senza troppe formalità.

Questa situazione va avanti da decenni e ogni anno peggiora. Non siamo più davanti a qualche inevitabile complicazione organizzativa, a un settembre particolarmente congestionato, a una stagione di adempimenti destinata a esaurirsi con l’avvio delle lezioni. Siamo davanti a una trasformazione progressiva del mestiere, che conserva il nome di insegnamento mentre una parte sempre più significativa e crescente del tempo e delle energie viene assorbita da tutto ciò che gli gira intorno. Insegnare significa preparare lezioni, studiare, leggere, aggiornarsi, costruire verifiche, correggere elaborati, comprendere le difficoltà degli studenti, trovare spiegazioni diverse quando quelle abituali non funzionano. Significa avere la disponibilità mentale per entrare in classe e accorgersi di ciò che accade, per seguire un ragazzo che fatica, per approfondire un argomento, per trasmettere non soltanto conoscenze, ma anche curiosità e strumenti di comprensione. È un lavoro intellettuale e umano, che richiede tempo, concentrazione e una continua elaborazione personale.

La qualità dell’insegnamento dipende anche dalla qualità del tempo che rimane all’insegnante per insegnare. La scuola-azienda contemporanea lo ha ormai dimenticato del tutto. A ogni problema corrisponde una procedura, a ogni esigenza un modulo, a ogni progetto una documentazione, a ogni attività un verbale, a ogni obiettivo una rendicontazione. Se qualcosa non funziona, si istituisce un gruppo di lavoro; se il gruppo deve dimostrare di aver lavorato, si convoca una riunione; se la riunione deve produrre risultati verificabili, si redige un documento. Poi si archivia tutto e, talvolta, il problema rimane esattamente dov’era.

Naturalmente, una parte della burocrazia è indispensabile: servono regole, trasparenza, tutela degli studenti, coordinamento, responsabilità definite. Il punto è capire quando gli strumenti cominciano a consumare la funzione che dovrebbero sostenere. Una riunione non diventa produttiva perché è stata convocata, una comunicazione non è efficace soltanto perché è stata inviata, un modulo non è utile per il solo fatto di essere compilato. Occorrerebbe chiedersi quanto tempo richiedano questi adempimenti, quali problemi risolvano e quali risultati concreti producano. Invece, nella scuola si è affermata una logica di accumulazione: si aggiungono obblighi senza eliminare quelli superflui, si introducono nuove procedure senza verificare le precedenti, si moltiplicano le comunicazioni senza preoccuparsi del carico complessivo che grava sui destinatari. Ogni singola richiesta sembra ragionevole, ogni scadenza appare gestibile, ogni riunione occupa soltanto un paio d’ore. È la loro somma a diventare insostenibile, insieme alla continua frammentazione dell’attenzione, alle interruzioni e alla necessità di tenere sotto controllo un flusso incessante di informazioni.

Digitalizzare tutto, del resto, non significa necessariamente semplificare. Può significare rendere più veloce la produzione delle richieste, moltiplicarne la frequenza e trasferire sugli insegnanti ulteriori operazioni. Chi invia una circolare impiega pochi minuti; chi la riceve deve leggerla, comprenderla, stabilire se lo riguarda, individuare eventuali scadenze e, quando necessario, agire. La facilità con cui si produce una comunicazione non coincide con la facilità con cui la si gestisce. Così, accanto al lavoro reale, cresce un secondo lavoro, che come Crono coi figli ha ormai divorato il primo: la documentazione del lavoro. Accanto alla lezione c’è la sua formalizzazione, accanto al progetto il suo monitoraggio, accanto all’attività svolta la dichiarazione che ne attesta lo svolgimento. Si finisce per confondere ciò che è facilmente registrabile con ciò che ha valore, dimenticando che si può compilare tutto correttamente e svolgere una lezione mediocre, così come si può fare un lavoro didattico straordinario senza che la sua qualità trovi una rappresentazione adeguata nei documenti prodotti.

Il paradosso è evidente: mentre si moltiplicano gli strumenti destinati a migliorare la scuola, si sottrae tempo a una delle condizioni essenziali di quel miglioramento. La preparazione didattica scivola nelle ore serali, la lettura personale diventa un lusso, la correzione dei compiti si accumula nei fine settimana, la concentrazione viene continuamente interrotta. Quando finalmente si arriva alla lezione del giorno successivo, bisogna trovare le energie che sono rimaste dopo aver soddisfatto tutto il resto. E il tempo naturalmente ha un costo, anche quando nessun bilancio lo registra: un costo fisico, mentale, familiare e professionale. Una scuola può continuare a funzionare grazie alla disponibilità supplementare dei suoi insegnanti, ma questo non dimostra che sia organizzata bene: dimostra che molte persone continuano a compensare con il proprio impegno le inefficienze del sistema. Se tutto viene comunque fatto, se le lezioni sono preparate, le verifiche corrette, le riunioni frequentate e i moduli compilati, l’organizzazione può perfino convincersi che il carico sia sostenibile. Scambia così il sacrificio individuale per efficienza collettiva.

A rendere tutto ancora più irritante c’è il riconoscimento economico. Alla professione vengono richieste competenze sempre più ampie, responsabilità crescenti, disponibilità continua e una quantità progressiva di attività collaterali, mentre gli stipendi rimangono perennemente inadeguati rispetto alla preparazione necessaria e alla complessità del lavoro. Si pretende che l’insegnante sia specialista disciplinare, educatore, valutatore, mediatore, progettista, referente, compilatore e interlocutore permanente di una pluralità di soggetti, confidando spesso nella sua coscienza professionale per assorbire ogni nuova incombenza. La vocazione, in questo quadro, rischia di diventare un alibi. Poiché insegnare è importante, si dà per scontato che l’insegnante possa trovare nella propria passione la compensazione per ciò che manca sul piano economico e organizzativo. Dovrebbe accettare qualche ora in più, qualche riunione aggiuntiva, qualche scadenza urgente, perché in fondo il suo lavoro riguarda il futuro dei ragazzi. Proprio perché riguarda il futuro dei ragazzi, meriterebbe condizioni migliori. La passione dovrebbe essere coltivata, non utilizzata come una riserva inesauribile con cui coprire le inefficienze dell’istituzione.

Il danno, infatti, riguarda anche gli studenti. Un insegnante che arriva in classe dopo una giornata amministrativamente congestionata può avere meno energie per spiegare, ascoltare, approfondire, correggere e trovare una strada diversa per chi non ha capito. Un consiglio di classe assorbito da adempimenti formali dispone di meno spazio per discutere seriamente delle difficoltà di un ragazzo. Ogni ora sottratta alla preparazione e alla riflessione didattica ha conseguenze, anche quando nessun documento è in grado di misurarle. La scuola consuma così proprio ciò che dovrebbe proteggere: la competenza, la curiosità intellettuale, l’attenzione e la disponibilità umana di chi insegna. Una professione può restare bellissima nel suo nucleo essenziale e diventare, nelle condizioni concrete in cui viene esercitata, sempre più logorante. È questa la contraddizione che molti insegnanti sperimentano da anni: continuare ad amare il proprio lavoro mentre diventa sempre più difficile trovare il tempo e le energie per svolgerlo bene.

La soluzione richiederebbe un cambiamento molto concreto ma radicale: eliminare gli adempimenti ridondanti, unificare le richieste, razionalizzare le comunicazioni, limitare le riunioni a quelle realmente necessarie, coordinare le scadenze e verificare periodicamente l’utilità delle procedure. Ogni nuova attività dovrebbe essere valutata anche in rapporto al carico già esistente, chiedendosi che cosa sia possibile semplificare o eliminare. La buona organizzazione consiste nel selezionare ciò che serve, distribuire le responsabilità e rendere possibile il lavoro, non nel riempire ogni spazio disponibile nell’agenda del personale. Dovremmo smettere, soprattutto, di confondere la scuola con la sua amministrazione. Il risultato più importante dell’insegnamento non è un documento archiviato, ma ciò che uno studente riesce a comprendere, leggere, interpretare e pensare autonomamente. Sono risultati che richiedono tempo, attenzione e continuità, e che nessuna moltiplicazione di moduli può produrre al posto di chi insegna.

Dopo un mese trascorso fra riunioni pomeridiane, form, circolari e decine di email quotidiane, è dunque legittimo provare una rabbia che va oltre il fastidio per l’ennesima incombenza. È la rabbia di chi vede progressivamente restringersi lo spazio della propria professione, anno dopo anno, senza che nessuno sembri disposto a interrogarsi seriamente sulle conseguenze. La sensazione è quella di dover difendere ogni giorno il tempo necessario per fare il lavoro per cui si è stati assunti. Nel frattempo la scuola continua a chiedere intelligenza, cultura, pazienza, sensibilità e responsabilità, offrendo condizioni sempre meno favorevoli per esercitarle e una retribuzione che non restituisce un riconoscimento proporzionato a ciò che viene richiesto. Il rischio è perdere progressivamente l’attrattiva della professione, scoraggiare chi vorrebbe intraprenderla e logorare chi continua a svolgerla con serietà.

Non serve idealizzare gli insegnanti, così come non serve fingere che ogni procedura sia inutile. Serve distinguere ciò che tutela e migliora il lavoro da ciò che si limita a consumarlo, riconoscendo che il tempo delle persone è una risorsa educativa e che sprecarlo significa impoverire la scuola. Una scuola che non protegge il tempo necessario per insegnare finisce per danneggiare proprio ciò che dovrebbe garantire. Il paradosso finale è tutto qui: abbiamo costruito un sistema che pretende di migliorare continuamente la scuola attraverso un numero crescente di attività, procedure e documenti, senza domandarsi abbastanza se stia diventando più difficile fare bene il lavoro fondamentale.

Hanno lasciato intatto il nome della professione, ne hanno moltiplicato gli obblighi, ne hanno peggiorato le condizioni economiche e ne hanno progressivamente ristretto lo spazio vitale. Poi si domandano perché gli insegnanti siano stanchi.

Ogni nuova attività dovrebbe essere valutata anche in rapporto al carico già esistente, chiedendosi che cosa sia possibile semplificare o eliminare. La buona organizzazione consiste nel selezionare ciò che serve, distribuire le responsabilità e rendere possibile il lavoro, non nel riempire ogni spazio disponibile nell’agenda del personale. Dovremmo smettere, soprattutto, di confondere la scuola con la sua amministrazione. Il risultato più importante dell’insegnamento non è un documento archiviato, ma ciò che uno studente riesce a comprendere, leggere, interpretare e pensare autonomamente. Sono risultati che richiedono tempo, attenzione e continuità, e che nessuna moltiplicazione di moduli può produrre al posto di chi insegna.

Dopo un mese trascorso fra riunioni pomeridiane, form, circolari e decine di email quotidiane, è dunque legittimo provare una rabbia che va oltre il fastidio per l’ennesima incombenza. È la rabbia di chi vede progressivamente restringersi lo spazio della propria professione, anno dopo anno, senza che nessuno sembri disposto a interrogarsi seriamente sulle conseguenze. La sensazione è quella di dover difendere ogni giorno il tempo necessario per fare il lavoro per cui si è stati assunti. Nel frattempo la scuola continua a chiedere intelligenza, cultura, pazienza, sensibilità e responsabilità, offrendo condizioni sempre meno favorevoli per esercitarle e una retribuzione che non restituisce un riconoscimento proporzionato a ciò che viene richiesto. Il rischio è perdere progressivamente l’attrattiva della professione, scoraggiare chi vorrebbe intraprenderla e logorare chi continua a svolgerla con serietà.

Non serve idealizzare gli insegnanti, così come non serve fingere che ogni procedura sia inutile. Serve distinguere ciò che tutela e migliora il lavoro da ciò che si limita a consumarlo, riconoscendo che il tempo delle persone è una risorsa educativa e che sprecarlo significa impoverire la scuola. Una scuola che non protegge il tempo necessario per insegnare finisce per danneggiare proprio ciò che dovrebbe garantire. Il paradosso finale è tutto qui: abbiamo costruito un sistema che pretende di migliorare continuamente la scuola attraverso un numero crescente di attività, procedure e documenti, senza domandarsi abbastanza se stia diventando più difficile fare bene il lavoro fondamentale.

Hanno lasciato intatto il nome della professione, ne hanno moltiplicato gli obblighi, ne hanno peggiorato le condizioni economiche e ne hanno progressivamente ristretto lo spazio vitale. Poi si domandano perché gli insegnanti siano stanchi.

full_text:
Astăzi, 14 octombrie 2026, a fost finalizată încărcarea manualelor, atât în format digital, cât și PDF, pe platforma dedicată, operațiune subsecventă semnării, în data de 12 octombrie, a acordurilor-cadru pentru manualele pentru clasa a IX-a declarate câștigătoare în urma licitațiilor, pentru 63 de discipline.

Reamintim, prin ordin de ministru au fost aprobate manualele școlare pentru clasa a IX-a declarate câștigătoare în urma licitațiilor (pentru 63 de discipline). Pentru alte 9 discipline au fost depuse contestații, iar procedura va continua după soluționarea acestora.

Ministrul Educației și Cercetării, Mihai Dimian:

„Le mulțumesc tuturor celor implicați, care, prin efortul lor, au redus durata procedurii de achiziție de la o medie de 10 luni la aproximativ 7 luni! Le mulțumesc pentru această activitate desfășurată inclusiv în perioade de weekend și vacanțe, pentru a duce la bun sfârșit cât mai repede etapele care au depins de noi. Pentru clasa a X-a am solicitat deja pregătirea documentației pentru procedura de achiziție, astfel încât manualele să poată fi disponibile în licee până în august 2027. Elevii și profesorii au nevoie de predictibilitate și de resursele necesare încă de la începutul anului școlar, iar pentru aceasta, fiecare etapă trebuie pregătită din timp.”

Următoarele etape în cadrul acestui proces sunt selecția manualelor de către școli, înregistrarea și centralizarea comenzilor. Comenzile de manuale vor fi în concordanță cu cifrele de școlarizare aprobate pentru anul școlar 2026 - 2027.

Pentru derularea procesului de înregistrare și de centralizare a comenzilor de manuale școlare, în conformitate cu Metodologia de achiziție a manualelor școlare pentru învățământul preuniversitar aprobată prin Ordinul de ministru nr. 3.333/2026 privind regimul manualelor școlare în învățământul preuniversitar, se va deschide și va putea fi utilizată aplicația web specifică disponibilă la nivelul unităților de învățământ, al ISJ/ISMB, al MEC-CNCE.
